newsitem.title: USA: Huge tax overhaul needed for 'orphan' DC-Brookings.
newsitem.headline: Huge tax overhaul needed for 'orphan' DC-Brookings.

text.p: Brookings Institution warned Tuesday that District of Columbia's tax system is severely "dysfunctional" and called on the city, its neighboring states and the U.S. government for a massive overhaul.

"The District of Columbia's revenue structure is collapsing -- but it can be fixed," an institute panel headed by former New York City finance chief Carol O'Cleireacain said in a 12-page report released at Brookings headquarters here.

Unlike other cities, D.C.'s tax base is severely restricted by federal law, O'Cleireacain said. There is no state aid, and the federal government -- the hometown industry -- is tax exempt, O'Cleireacain said.
"Truly, this is an orphaned capital," she said. "Increasingly, businesses and residents are leaving town."
O'Cleireacain and a team of four researchers proposed that four D.C. business taxes be eliminated, including personal property and corporate income taxes.
Also, commercial property tax revenues should be cut by 27 percent, with five classes reduced to two, the report says.

And personal income taxes should be cut by 30 percent, which means that residents with gross incomes of less than $200,000 would see tax cuts, and 36 percent of D.C. residents would pay no income tax, the report says.
"The new income tax would be a single rate of 28 percent of federal liability," said Brookings, which said the Internal Revenue Service should take over D.C. tax collection and enforcement.
The Brookings team said federal and state governments should increase aid to the struggling District in three ways.

First, the federal government should make an annual $382 million payment to D.C. as compensation for revenue the city loses to so many tax-exempt properties, Brookings said. That could trigger tax cuts for all city propertyholders.
Second, neighboring states should kick in $434 million to D.C. annually, which is roughly what cities the size of D.C. within their own borders get in state aid, Brookings said.
Third, the federal government should share more of D.C.'s bills for Medicaid reimbursement, welfare and other such costs, giving the city an added $378 million, Brookings said.
"The plan is fair and manageable," O'Cleireacain said. "It is the least that the nation can do to ensure the viability of its own capital city."
Brookings released the report as the White House prepared to announce a massive aid package for the ailing District.

Under the plan, the U.S. government would pay 70 percent of the city's Medicaid bills instead of the current 50 percent and it would assume full payment of a nearly $5 billion unfunded pension liability for some city workers that D.C. inherited from the U.S. when it won Home Rule in 1974, the source said.

Also, the U.S. would assume responsibility for the city's roughly 7,000 jailed felons, forfeit an annual $660 million payment-in-lieu-of-taxes from the U.S., and announce a package of tax incentives aimed at encouraging businesses and jobs in the city, the source said.
Charlene Drew Jarvis, acting chair of D.C.'s 13-member city council, was cautiously optimistic about the President's upcoming plan.

"This ushers in a new era for the District in its relationship with the federal government," Jarvis said. She said she is tempted to "jump for joy" but wants to see White House numbers first, particularly the White House's plan to wipe out the city's $660 million annual federal payment. "The devil is in the details," Jarvis told Reuters.
